sk: भृगुर्वै वारुणिः वरुणं पितरमुपससार अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति तस्मा एतत्प्रोवाच अन्नं प्राणं चक्षुः श्रोत्रं मनो वाचमिति तꣳ होवाच यतो वा इमानि भूतानि जायन्ते येन जातानि जीवन्ति यत्प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्ति तद्विजिज्ञासस्व तद्ब्रह्मेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा ||
ro: bhṛguḥ · vai · vāruṇiḥ · varuṇaṁ · pitaram · upasasāra · adhīhi · bhagavo · brahma · iti · tasmai · etat · provāca · annaṁ · prāṇaṁ · cakṣuḥ · śrotraṁ · manaḥ · vācam · iti · taṁ · ha · uvāca · yataḥ · vā · imāni · bhūtāni · jāyante · yena · jātāni · jīvanti · yat · prayanti · abhisaṁviśanti · tat · vijijñāsasva · tat · brahma · iti · saḥ · tapaḥ · atapyata · saḥ · tapaḥ · taptvā ||
hi: भृगु (Bhrigu) वारुणि (son of Varuṇa / वरुण-पुत्र) ने वरुण (Varuṇa) पिता (father) के पास (उपससार) गया (approached)। 'अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्म' ('Teach me, revered sir, Brahman / भगवन् मुझे ब्रह्म पढ़ाइए') इति [कहा]। उसको (तस्मै) यह (एतत्) प्रोवाच (told / बताया): 'अन्नम् (food), प्राणम् (breath), चक्षुः (sight), श्रोत्रम् (hearing), मनः (mind), वाचम् (speech)' — [ये ब्रह्म को जानने के साधन हैं] इति। उससे (तम्) कहा (ह उवाच): 'जिससे (यतः) ये (इमानि) सभी भूत (beings / प्राणी) जायन्ते (are born / जन्म लेते हैं), जिससे (येन) जन्मे हुए (जातानि) जीवन्ति (live / जीवित रहते हैं), जिसमें (यत्) प्रयन्ति (departing / जाते हुए) अभिसंविशन्ति (they enter / प्रवेश करते हैं) — उसे (तत्) विजिज्ञासस्व (seek to know / जानने की इच्छा करो) — वही (तत्) ब्रह्म (Brahman) है।' उसने (सः) तपः (tapas / austerity) अतप्यत (performed / तपा)। उसने तप कर (तपः तप्त्वा) —
en: Bhrigu, the son of Varuṇa (vāruṇi), approached (upasasāra) his father Varuṇa. 'Teach me, revered sir, Brahman (adhīhi bhagavo brahma),' [he said]. To him, [Varuṇa] declared this: 'Food (anna), breath (prāṇa), sight (cakṣus), hearing (śrotra), mind (manas), speech (vāc)' — [these are the means of knowing Brahman]. He said to him: 'That from which (yataḥ) these beings are born (jāyante), that by which (yena), once born, they live (jīvanti), that into which (yat), departing, they enter (abhisaṁviśanti) — seek to know that (vijijñāsasva). That is Brahman.' He performed tapas (austerity). Having performed tapas —

ws.h: पास गया / समीप गया / approached
ws.e: approached — upa + sa + √sṛ (to go); the formal approach of a student to a teacher; in the Vedic tradition, upasadana (approaching) is the ritual act of requesting instruction — the student goes TO the teacher, demonstrating humility and readiness

ws.h: पढ़ाइए / सिखाइए / teach me / instruct me
ws.e: teach me / instruct me — adhi + √i (to go/study); imperative form = 'please teach'; the traditional formula of the student requesting instruction from the guru; cf. 'adhīhi bhagavo' in the Chāndogya (4.4.5) where Satyakāma approaches Haridrumata Gautama

ws.h: जानने की इच्छा करो / seek to know / desire to know thoroughly
ws.e: seek to know / desire to know thoroughly — vi + √jñā (to know) in the desiderative (jijñāsa) = the desire to know; imperative = 'seek to know!'; Varuṇa does NOT give Bhrigu the answer — he gives him the METHOD: inquiry through tapas (austerity). The desiderative form emphasises that knowing Brahman requires active, sustained DESIRE to know, not passive reception

ws.h: प्रवेश करते हैं / लौट कर समा जाते हैं / they enter into / they merge back
ws.e: they enter into / they merge back — abhi + sam + √viś (to enter); beings RETURN to Brahman at death/dissolution — they 'enter back into' the source from which they emerged; the triple formula (born from, live by, return to) is the defining characteristic of Brahman

gr: Bhrigu approaches Varuṇa — the great inquiry begins: this opening mantra sets the stage for the entire Bhṛguvallī. The student: Bhṛgu, son of Varuṇa — approaching his own father as guru. The father-son teacher-student relationship is a pattern in the Upanishads (cf. Uddālaka-Śvetaketu in the Chāndogya, Yama-Naciketa in the Kaṭha). The request: 'adhīhi bhagavo brahma' — the simplest, most direct request possible: 'Teach me Brahman.' Varuṇa's first response: Varuṇa gives Bhrigu the INSTRUMENTS of knowing — anna (food), prāṇa (breath), cakṣus (sight), śrotra (hearing), manas (mind), vāc (speech). These are not Brahman itself but the faculties through which Brahman can be investigated. The definition of Brahman: Varuṇa then gives the famous triple formula: 'That from which beings are born (janma-kāraṇa), that by which they live (sthiti-kāraṇa), that into which they enter at the end (laya-kāraṇa) — THAT is Brahman.' This threefold causality (origin, sustenance, dissolution) is the functional definition of Brahman — not what Brahman IS in itself, but what Brahman DOES. The method: 'vijijñāsasva' — SEEK TO KNOW. Varuṇa does NOT simply tell Bhrigu the answer. He gives Bhrigu a method: (1) a definition/criterion (the triple formula), (2) a practice (tapas = austerity/contemplation), and (3) freedom to discover for himself. Tapas: Bhrigu's response is tapas — concentrated contemplation/austerity. This will be his tool for each successive realisation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.1.1 — The triple formula 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante, yena jātāni jīvanti, yat prayanty abhisaṁviśanti' echoes the Brahma Sūtra's opening definition (BS 1.1.2): 'janmādy asya yataḥ' (that from which the birth etc. [of this universe proceeds]). Bādarāyaṇa is widely understood to be paraphrasing this very Taittirīya passage. The six faculties mentioned by Varuṇa (anna, prāṇa, cakṣus, śrotra, manas, vāc) are not random — they represent the full range of human experience: food (physical), breath (vital), sight and hearing (sensory), mind (mental), speech (expressive). Varuṇa is saying: use ALL your faculties to investigate Brahman. The pedagogical method — giving the criterion and the method but not the answer — is the Taittirīya's distinctive approach. Unlike the Chāndogya where Uddālaka TELLS Śvetaketu 'tat tvam asi,' Varuṇa makes Bhrigu DISCOVER Brahman through his own tapas. Each time Bhrigu returns with an answer, Varuṇa neither confirms nor denies but simply says 'do more tapas' — until Bhrigu arrives at the final answer himself.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — वरुण = गुरु (teacher)। भृगु = जिज्ञासु शिष्य (inquiring student)। 'यतो वा इमानि...' = ब्रह्म का लक्षण (definition of Brahman) = जगत् का जन्म-स्थिति-लय कारण (cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world)। 'विजिज्ञासस्व' = ब्रह्म-जिज्ञासा (desire to know Brahman) = वेदान्त का प्रारम्भ (beginning of Vedānta)। तपस् = चिन्तन / मनन (contemplation / reflection)।
advaita.en: Shankara says Varuṇa = the teacher. Bhrigu = the inquiring student. 'Yato vā imāni...' = the definition of Brahman = the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world. 'Vijijñāsasva' = the desire to know Brahman = the beginning of Vedānta. Tapas = contemplation / reflection.
advaita.ins: Bhrigu asks his father: teach me Brahman. Varuṇa gives the criterion: that from which everything is born, by which everything lives, into which everything returns. Then the crucial instruction: SEEK to know it. Not 'here is the answer' but 'go find it through tapas.' The journey begins.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'यतो वा इमानि...' = भगवान् = जगत् का कारण (God = the cause of the world) — उत्पत्ति (creation), स्थिति (sustenance), लय (dissolution) — सब भगवान् से। 'विजिज्ञासस्व' = भगवान् को जानने का अभ्यास (practice of knowing God)। तपस् = भगवद्-ध्यान (meditation on God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'yato vā imāni...' = God = the cause of the world — creation, sustenance, dissolution — all from God. 'Vijijñāsasva' = the practice of knowing God. Tapas = meditation on God.
vishisht.ins: Everything is born from God, lives by God, returns to God. That triple relationship IS the definition of Brahman. Varuṇa tells Bhrigu: seek to know THAT — through tapas, through devoted contemplation. The answer isn't given — it must be discovered through practice.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — भृगु-वरुण संवाद = चेतना की आत्म-खोज (self-discovery of consciousness)। 'यतो वा इमानि...' = चेतना = सबका उद्गम (source of all), सबका आधार (support of all), सबका गन्तव्य (goal of all)। तपस् = चेतना की एकाग्रता (concentration of consciousness) — ज्ञान का साधन।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the Bhrigu-Varuṇa dialogue = the self-discovery of consciousness. 'Yato vā imāni...' = consciousness = the source, support, and goal of all. Tapas = concentration of consciousness — the means of knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: Bhrigu's inquiry is consciousness seeking to know itself. The criterion: that from which all emerges, by which all lives, into which all returns. The method: tapas — concentrated consciousness turning inward. The Bhṛguvallī is the story of consciousness discovering its own depths, layer by layer.

dp.q: 🔍 The triple formula — Brahman as origin, sustenance, and goal
dp.a: Varuṇa's definition of Brahman — 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante, yena jātāni jīvanti, yat prayanty abhisaṁviśanti' — is one of the most important functional definitions in the Upanishads: The three aspects: (1) Janma-kāraṇa (cause of origin): 'yataḥ imāni bhūtāni jāyante' — that FROM WHICH all beings are born. Brahman is the material and/or efficient cause of creation. (2) Sthiti-kāraṇa (cause of sustenance): 'yena jātāni jīvanti' — that BY WHICH, once born, they live. Brahman is not just the creator but the sustainer — the ongoing support of all existence. (3) Laya-kāraṇa (cause of dissolution): 'yat prayanty abhisaṁviśanti' — that INTO WHICH, departing, they enter. Brahman is the final destination — all beings return to their source. The Brahma Sūtra connection: Bādarāyaṇa's Brahma Sūtra 1.1.2 — 'janmādy asya yataḥ' (that from which the birth etc. [of this universe proceeds]) — is widely understood as a direct paraphrase of this Taittirīya passage. This makes the Bhṛguvallī's definition foundational for all subsequent Vedāntic philosophy. The method, not the answer: Varuṇa gives Bhrigu a CRITERION, not a conclusion. He says: whatever satisfies this triple test — origin, sustenance, dissolution — THAT is Brahman. Now go find it. This turns the student from a passive recipient into an active inquirer. Bhrigu must test each candidate (food, breath, mind, knowledge, bliss) against this criterion. The universal scope: the formula covers ALL beings ('imāni bhūtāni') and ALL phases of existence (birth, life, death/dissolution). Nothing falls outside it. Whatever is the universal cause of all these — that alone is Brahman.

dp.q: 🔍 'Vijijñāsasva' — the pedagogy of self-discovery
dp.a: Varuṇa's instruction 'vijijñāsasva' (seek to know) introduces a distinctive pedagogical method — one that contrasts sharply with the 'direct teaching' approach of other Upanishads: The Bhṛguvallī method: (1) Teacher gives the CRITERION (the triple formula). (2) Teacher gives the METHOD (tapas). (3) Student DISCOVERS the answer through practice. (4) Student returns with each successive realisation. (5) Teacher implicitly redirects ('tapas is Brahman — do more tapas'). (6) Student goes deeper until reaching the final answer. Compare with other Upanishads: (a) Chāndogya: Uddālaka TELLS Śvetaketu: 'tat tvam asi' (you are that) — a direct declaration. (b) Kaṭha: Yama TEACHES Naciketa step by step — a structured lecture. (c) Bṛhadāraṇyaka: Yājñavalkya EXPLAINS through dialogue — question and answer. The Bhṛguvallī is unique: Varuṇa does NOT tell Bhrigu what Brahman is. He gives him the tools and says: find out for yourself. Why this matters: (a) Self-discovered knowledge is deeper than received knowledge — what you find through your own tapas becomes part of you. (b) The progressive discoveries (anna → prāṇa → manas → vijñāna → ānanda) mirror the five-sheath analysis of the Brahmānandavallī — but discovered from the OUTSIDE IN rather than taught from the inside out. (c) The method validates PROCESS over product — the journey of discovery IS the teaching, not just the final answer. Tapas as the instrument: tapas (austerity/concentrated contemplation) is the means of each discovery. This is not physical penance but focused, sustained inquiry — the mind concentrated on a question until the answer reveals itself.

sk: अन्नं ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात् अन्नाद्ध्येव खल्विमानि भूतानि जायन्ते अन्नेन जातानि जीवन्ति अन्नं प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्तीति तद्विज्ञाय पुनरेव वरुणं पितरमुपससार अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति तꣳ होवाच तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व तपो ब्रह्मेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा ||
ro: annaṁ · brahma · iti · vyajānāt · annāt · hi · eva · khalu · imāni · bhūtāni · jāyante · annena · jātāni · jīvanti · annaṁ · prayanti · abhisaṁviśanti · iti · tat · vijñāya · punaḥ · eva · varuṇaṁ · pitaram · upasasāra · adhīhi · bhagavo · brahma · iti · taṁ · ha · uvāca · tapasā · brahma · vijijñāsasva · tapaḥ · brahma · iti · saḥ · tapaḥ · atapyata · saḥ · tapaḥ · taptvā ||
hi: अन्नम् (food) = ब्रह्म (Brahman) इति (thus) व्यजानात् (he understood / उसने जाना)। अन्न से ही (अन्नात् हि एव खलु) ये (इमानि) सभी भूत (beings) जायन्ते (are born / जन्म लेते हैं)। अन्न से (अन्नेन) जन्मे हुए (जातानि) जीवन्ति (live / जीवित रहते हैं)। अन्न में (अन्नम्) जाते हुए (प्रयन्ति) अभिसंविशन्ति (they enter back / प्रवेश करते हैं)। वह (तत्) विज्ञाय (having known / जान कर) पुनः (again / फिर से) ही (एव) वरुण पिता के पास (उपससार) गया। 'अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्म' ('Teach me Brahman / मुझे ब्रह्म पढ़ाइए')। उससे (तम्) कहा (ह उवाच): 'तपसा (by tapas / तप से) ब्रह्म (Brahman को) विजिज्ञासस्व (seek to know / जानने की इच्छा करो)। तपः (tapas) = ब्रह्म (Brahman) है।' उसने (सः) तपः अतप्यत (performed tapas / तप किया)। तप कर (तपः तप्त्वा) —
en: He understood (vyajānāt): 'Food (anna) is Brahman.' For from food indeed (annāt hi eva khalu) these beings are born; by food, once born, they live; into food, departing, they enter. Having known (vijñāya) that, he again (punaḥ) approached his father Varuṇa. 'Teach me, revered sir, Brahman.' He said to him: 'By tapas (austerity), seek to know Brahman (tapasā brahma vijijñāsasva). Tapas is Brahman (tapo brahma).' He performed tapas. Having performed tapas —

ws.h: जाना / समझा / he understood / he realised
ws.e: he understood / he realised — vi + √jñā (to know); aorist form = he came to know, he realised; Bhrigu arrived at this understanding through tapas (contemplation), not through being told; each successive vyajānāt represents a deeper realisation

ws.h: निश्चय ही / indeed / certainly
ws.e: indeed / certainly / verily — an emphatic particle; reinforces that food genuinely satisfies the triple criterion: beings ARE born from food, DO live by food, DO return to food

ws.h: तप ही ब्रह्म है / tapas is Brahman
ws.e: tapas is Brahman — Varuṇa identifies the METHOD of knowing with the OBJECT of knowing; tapas (concentrated contemplation/austerity) is itself Brahman — the practice of seeking Brahman IS Brahman; this also serves as encouragement: do MORE tapas

gr: First realisation — food (anna) is Brahman: Bhrigu's first discovery through tapas is that FOOD is Brahman. The reasoning: food satisfies Varuṇa's triple criterion: (1) Beings are born from food — all life depends on nourishment for coming into being. (2) Beings live by food — they are sustained by eating. (3) Beings return to food — at death, the body returns to earth and becomes nourishment for other life. Is this wrong? Bhrigu's answer is not FALSE — it is INCOMPLETE. Food IS a legitimate candidate for Brahman at the physical level. The Brahmānandavallī (2.2) praises food extensively ('annāt vai prajāḥ prajāyante'). Food IS the origin, sustainer, and goal of physical existence. But food is the OUTERMOST layer — the annamaya kośa. There are deeper realities. Varuṇa's response: crucially, Varuṇa does NOT say 'you are wrong.' He says: 'tapasā brahma vijijñāsasva — tapo brahma' — 'seek to know Brahman through tapas; tapas is Brahman.' This is a gentle redirection: your answer is valid but not complete. Go deeper. The identification 'tapo brahma' (tapas is Brahman) is both instruction (use tapas to find Brahman) and hint (the answer lies in the process itself). The pattern established: this mantra establishes the pattern for mantras 2-6: Bhrigu realises → returns → asks again → Varuṇa says 'do more tapas' → Bhrigu does tapas → next realisation. Each cycle takes him one layer deeper.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.2.1 — Bhrigu's first realisation (anna = Brahman) directly corresponds to the annamaya kośa of the Brahmānandavallī (2.2). The Bhṛguvallī can be read as the EXPERIENTIAL counterpart of the Brahmānandavallī's THEORETICAL analysis — the same five layers (anna, prāṇa, manas, vijñāna, ānanda) discovered through personal practice rather than taught through systematic exposition. Varuṇa's response 'tapo brahma' is ambiguous by design: (a) It can mean 'by tapas, know Brahman' — tapas = the method. (b) It can mean 'tapas IS Brahman' — tapas = the reality itself. Shankara reads the redirection as implicit correction: Varuṇa's silence about whether anna = Brahman is correct indicates that it is NOT the final answer. If it were correct, Varuṇa would have said so. His instruction to do more tapas implies: go deeper.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — भृगु का प्रथम ज्ञान: अन्न = ब्रह्म — अपूर्ण (incomplete) — क्योंकि अन्न = जड़ (inert) — चेतन (conscious) नहीं। वरुण का 'तपो ब्रह्म' = अप्रत्यक्ष खण्डन (implicit refutation) — यदि अन्न ही ब्रह्म होता तो वरुण कहते 'सही है' — परन्तु उसने कहा 'और तप करो' = 'और गहरे जाओ।'
advaita.en: Shankara says Bhrigu's first knowledge: anna = Brahman — incomplete — because anna = inert — not conscious. Varuṇa's 'tapo brahma' = implicit refutation — if anna were truly Brahman, Varuṇa would have confirmed; instead he said 'do more tapas' = 'go deeper.'
advaita.ins: Food seems like Brahman — everything is born from it, lives by it, returns to it. But food is inert — it doesn't know itself. When Bhrigu brings this answer, Varuṇa doesn't say 'right' or 'wrong.' He says: do more tapas. That silence IS the teaching.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — अन्न = ब्रह्म — आंशिक सत्य (partial truth) — अन्न = भगवान् का स्थूल रूप (God's gross form)। वरुण = भृगु को गहनतर (deeper) दर्शन के लिए प्रेरित करते हैं — 'तपो ब्रह्म' = ध्यान से भगवान् का अन्तरंग रूप (inner form of God through meditation)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says anna = Brahman — partial truth — anna = God's gross form. Varuṇa directs Bhrigu toward a deeper vision — 'tapo brahma' = the inner form of God through meditation.
vishisht.ins: Bhrigu's first insight is not wrong — food IS God's form, the grossest expression of the Divine. But it's only the surface. Varuṇa pushes him deeper: use tapas to find God's subtler forms. Each layer of reality is God — but the inner layers are more luminous.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — अन्न = भौतिक चेतना (physical/material consciousness) = चेतना का सबसे स्थूल स्तर। भृगु का प्रथम दर्शन = पदार्थ (matter) में ब्रह्म (Brahman in matter)। 'तपो ब्रह्म' = चेतना की एकाग्रता = गहनतर स्तरों का द्वार (gateway to deeper planes)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says anna = physical/material consciousness = the grossest plane of consciousness. Bhrigu's first vision = Brahman in matter. 'Tapo brahma' = concentration of consciousness = the gateway to deeper planes.
aurobindo.ins: Bhrigu's first discovery: matter is Brahman — consciousness in its most material form. This is not wrong — it IS consciousness. But it's the first layer. Tapas — concentrated consciousness turning inward — will reveal subtler, more luminous planes. The journey inward begins.

dp.q: 🔍 Anna as Brahman — the physical layer
dp.a: Bhrigu's first realisation — anna (food) = Brahman — represents the discovery of Brahman at the physical level: The logic: food satisfies Varuṇa's triple criterion perfectly at the material level: (a) All beings are BORN from food — life requires nourishment from the very first cell. (b) All beings LIVE by food — without eating, no creature survives. (c) All beings RETURN to food — at death, the body decomposes and becomes nourishment for plants and other organisms. The cycle is complete. Why it corresponds to the annamaya kośa: this first realisation maps exactly onto the Brahmānandavallī's first sheath — the annamaya kośa (the self made of food). Bhrigu is rediscovering through personal inquiry what the Brahmānandavallī taught theoretically. Why it is incomplete: food satisfies the criterion at the physical level but misses the deeper question. Food is INERT (jaḍa) — it does not know itself, it does not intend anything, it does not have consciousness. If Brahman is the ultimate reality, it must account for consciousness, not just matter. Food explains the body but not the mind, not awareness, not bliss. The Taittirīya's affirmation of matter: importantly, the Bhṛguvallī does NOT dismiss food. It does not say 'food is NOT Brahman.' It says food is Brahman — but not the WHOLE of Brahman. There are deeper layers. This is characteristic of the Taittirīya's approach: each layer is affirmed, not rejected, as the inquiry goes deeper.

dp.q: 🔍 Varuṇa's pedagogical genius — neither confirming nor denying
dp.a: Varuṇa's response to each of Bhrigu's realisations follows a remarkable pattern: he neither confirms nor denies, but redirects through tapas: The pattern: Bhrigu arrives with an answer. Varuṇa says: 'tapasā brahma vijijñāsasva — tapo brahma' ('seek Brahman through tapas — tapas is Brahman'). He does not say 'correct.' He does not say 'incorrect.' He says: go deeper. Why this works: (a) Preservation of the student's agency: if Varuṇa said 'wrong,' Bhrigu would feel discouraged. If he said 'right,' Bhrigu would stop inquiring. By saying neither, he keeps the inquiry alive. (b) Honouring partial truth: each of Bhrigu's answers IS true — at its level. Anna IS Brahman — at the physical level. Prāṇa IS Brahman — at the vital level. By not denying these, Varuṇa honours the truth in each realisation while pointing to something deeper. (c) The hint in the instruction: 'tapo brahma' — tapas IS Brahman. If Bhrigu has already found Brahman (in food), why is he being told to do more tapas? The instruction to continue implies: your answer is not yet complete. The fact that the journey continues IS the feedback. The contrast with direct teaching: Uddālaka tells Śvetaketu: 'tat tvam asi' — nine times, directly. Yama tells Naciketa the answer outright. But Varuṇa makes Bhrigu WORK for each insight. The result: Bhrigu's knowledge is self-won, not received. It transforms him from within because he discovered it himself.

sk: प्राणो ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात् प्राणाद्ध्येव खल्विमानि भूतानि जायन्ते प्राणेन जातानि जीवन्ति प्राणं प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्तीति तद्विज्ञाय पुनरेव वरुणं पितरमुपससार अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति तꣳ होवाच तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व तपो ब्रह्मेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा ||
ro: prāṇaḥ · brahma · iti · vyajānāt · prāṇāt · hi · eva · khalu · imāni · bhūtāni · jāyante · prāṇena · jātāni · jīvanti · prāṇaṁ · prayanti · abhisaṁviśanti · iti · tat · vijñāya · punaḥ · eva · varuṇaṁ · pitaram · upasasāra · adhīhi · bhagavo · brahma · iti · taṁ · ha · uvāca · tapasā · brahma · vijijñāsasva · tapaḥ · brahma · iti · saḥ · tapaḥ · atapyata · saḥ · tapaḥ · taptvā ||
hi: प्राणः (breath / प्राण) = ब्रह्म (Brahman) इति (thus) व्यजानात् (he understood / उसने जाना)। प्राण से ही (प्राणात् हि एव खलु) ये (इमानि) सभी भूत (beings) जायन्ते (are born / जन्म लेते हैं)। प्राण से (प्राणेन) जन्मे हुए (जातानि) जीवन्ति (live / जीवित रहते हैं)। प्राण में (प्राणम्) जाते हुए (प्रयन्ति) अभिसंविशन्ति (they enter back / प्रवेश करते हैं)। वह (तत्) विज्ञाय (having known) पुनः ही वरुण पिता के पास गया। 'अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्म' ('Teach me Brahman')। उससे कहा: 'तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व। तपो ब्रह्म।' उसने तपः किया। तप कर —
en: He understood (vyajānāt): 'Breath (prāṇa) is Brahman.' For from breath indeed these beings are born; by breath, once born, they live; into breath, departing, they enter. Having known that, he again approached his father Varuṇa. 'Teach me, revered sir, Brahman.' He said to him: 'By tapas, seek to know Brahman. Tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas. Having performed tapas —

ws.h: प्राण / श्वास / जीवन-शक्ति / breath / life-force
ws.e: breath / life-force — from pra + √an (to breathe); not just physical breathing but the vital force that animates all life; prāṇa is subtler than anna (food) — it is the ENERGY that makes the food-body alive; corresponds to the prāṇamaya kośa (breath-sheath) of the Brahmānandavallī

gr: Second realisation — breath (prāṇa) is Brahman: Bhrigu's second tapas yields a deeper insight: BREATH is Brahman. The reasoning: prāṇa satisfies the triple criterion at the vital level: (1) Beings are born from breath — life begins with the first breath; without vital energy, no organism can come into existence. (2) Beings live by breath — the continuity of breathing IS the continuity of life. (3) Beings return to breath — at death, the individual prāṇa merges back into the cosmic prāṇa. Deeper than food: prāṇa is a step beyond anna because: (a) Prāṇa ANIMATES food — the food-body is alive only because of breath. A corpse is made of food but has no prāṇa. (b) Prāṇa is subtler — it cannot be seen or touched, yet it pervades every cell of the living body. (c) Prāṇa is more essential — you can survive without food for weeks, but without breath for only minutes. Still incomplete: prāṇa explains LIFE but not CONSCIOUSNESS. A person under deep anaesthesia breathes (has prāṇa) but has no awareness. Brahman, as the ultimate reality, must include the capacity for knowing — not just living. Hence Varuṇa's familiar instruction: do more tapas.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.3.1 — Bhrigu's second realisation (prāṇa = Brahman) corresponds to the prāṇamaya kośa of the Brahmānandavallī (2.3). The pattern is now established: each realisation will correspond exactly to one of the five sheaths, in order from outer to inner. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka's 'contest of the prāṇas' (6.1.1-14) demonstrates prāṇa's supremacy among the vital faculties — when prāṇa threatens to leave the body, all other faculties beg it to stay. This supports prāṇa's candidacy as Brahman. But prāṇa's limitation is clear: it operates even in deep sleep and coma, where there is no consciousness — it is 'alive' but not 'aware.' Brahman must include both.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण = ब्रह्म — अन्न से सूक्ष्मतर (subtler than food) — परन्तु अपूर्ण — क्योंकि प्राण = जड़ शक्ति (inert force) — ज्ञान (consciousness) रहित। सुषुप्ति (deep sleep) में प्राण चलता है — चेतना नहीं। अतः प्राण = ब्रह्म नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says prāṇa = Brahman — subtler than food — but incomplete — because prāṇa = an inert force — devoid of consciousness. In deep sleep, breath continues but consciousness does not. Therefore prāṇa ≠ Brahman.
advaita.ins: Bhrigu goes deeper: breath, not food, is Brahman. Everything is born from vital energy, lives by it, returns to it. True — but breath is a blind force. It operates without knowing itself. The unconscious person still breathes. So: do more tapas.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण = भगवान् का प्राण-रूप (God as life-force) — अन्न से गहनतर — परन्तु भगवान् का पूर्ण रूप नहीं। प्रत्येक स्तर = भगवान् का एक आयाम (one dimension of God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says prāṇa = God as life-force — deeper than food — but not God's complete form. Each level = one dimension of God.
vishisht.ins: Bhrigu discovers God as life-force — subtler than food, more essential. Everything breathes by God's breath. But God is more than just the force of life — there are inner dimensions still to discover.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण = प्राणिक चेतना (vital consciousness) — भौतिक से सूक्ष्मतर — जीवन-शक्ति = चेतना का दूसरा स्तर। परन्तु प्राणिक चेतना = अन्ध (blind) — दिशा-हीन — मानसिक चेतना (mental consciousness) इसे दिशा देती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says prāṇa = vital consciousness — subtler than physical — life-force = the second plane of consciousness. But vital consciousness = blind — directionless — mental consciousness gives it direction.
aurobindo.ins: The second discovery: life-force is Brahman — consciousness as vital energy, animating everything. But vital consciousness is blind — it pushes without seeing. There must be a knowing principle behind the living principle. The inquiry continues inward.

dp.q: 🔍 The progressive deepening — from anna to prāṇa
dp.a: The transition from anna (food) to prāṇa (breath) as Brahman illustrates the Bhṛguvallī's method of progressive interiorisation: Why prāṇa is deeper than anna: (a) Dependence: the food-body depends on breath — without prāṇa, the food-body is a corpse. But breath does not depend on any particular food — it continues whether you have eaten or not. The more fundamental principle is the one on which the other depends. (b) Subtlety: food is gross — visible, tangible, measurable. Breath is subtle — invisible, felt but not seen, pervading the body without being locatable in any single organ. The subtler is closer to Brahman. (c) Universality: not all beings eat the same food, but all living beings breathe (in some form — even plants exchange gases). Breath is more universal than food. Why prāṇa still falls short: prāṇa explains LIFE but not AWARENESS. A ventilator can make a body breathe without the person being conscious. Prāṇa is a force (śakti) but not a knower (jñātṛ). If Brahman is the ultimate reality — 'satyaṁ jñānam anantam' (truth, knowledge, infinite) as the Brahmānandavallī declares — it must include the dimension of KNOWING, not just living. The pattern: each successive answer is TRUE at its level but INCOMPLETE. Anna is true for the physical. Prāṇa is true for the vital. But truth is not yet exhausted. The inquiry must go on.

dp.q: 🔍 The parallel with the five sheaths
dp.a: Bhrigu's progressive realisations exactly mirror the five-sheath (pañca-kośa) analysis of the Brahmānandavallī — but discovered experientially rather than taught theoretically: The correspondence: (1) Anna (food) = Annamaya kośa (food-sheath) — Brahmānandavallī 2.2. (2) Prāṇa (breath) = Prāṇamaya kośa (breath-sheath) — Brahmānandavallī 2.3. (3) Manas (mind) — coming next = Manomaya kośa — Brahmānandavallī 2.4. (4) Vijñāna (knowledge) = Vijñānamaya kośa — Brahmānandavallī 2.5. (5) Ānanda (bliss) = Ānandamaya kośa — Brahmānandavallī 2.6. Two methods, one truth: the Brahmānandavallī TEACHES the five sheaths through systematic exposition — the teacher describes each layer and its structure (bird-shape, parts, support). The Bhṛguvallī makes the student DISCOVER the same five layers through personal inquiry and tapas. Both arrive at the same destination: ānanda (bliss) as the innermost reality. The pedagogical insight: the Taittirīya Upanishad presents the same truth TWICE — once as theory (Brahmānandavallī), once as practice (Bhṛguvallī). This dual presentation ensures that the teaching is both intellectually understood and experientially discovered. Neither alone is sufficient — you need both map and journey.

sk: मनो ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात् मनसो ह्येव खल्विमानि भूतानि जायन्ते मनसा जातानि जीवन्ति मनः प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्तीति तद्विज्ञाय पुनरेव वरुणं पितरमुपससार अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति तꣳ होवाच तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व तपो ब्रह्मेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा ||
ro: manaḥ · brahma · iti · vyajānāt · manasaḥ · hi · eva · khalu · imāni · bhūtāni · jāyante · manasā · jātāni · jīvanti · manaḥ · prayanti · abhisaṁviśanti · iti · tat · vijñāya · punaḥ · eva · varuṇaṁ · pitaram · upasasāra · adhīhi · bhagavo · brahma · iti · taṁ · ha · uvāca · tapasā · brahma · vijijñāsasva · tapaḥ · brahma · iti · saḥ · tapaḥ · atapyata · saḥ · tapaḥ · taptvā ||
hi: मनः (mind / मन) = ब्रह्म इति व्यजानात् (he understood / उसने जाना)। मन से ही ये सभी भूत जायन्ते (are born)। मन से जातानि जीवन्ति (live)। मन में प्रयन्ति अभिसंविशन्ति (they enter back)। वह विज्ञाय पुनः वरुण पिता के पास गया। 'अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्म'। उससे कहा: 'तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व। तपो ब्रह्म।' उसने तपः किया। तप कर —
en: He understood: 'Mind (manas) is Brahman.' For from mind indeed these beings are born; by mind, once born, they live; into mind, departing, they enter. Having known that, he again approached his father Varuṇa. 'Teach me, revered sir, Brahman.' He said to him: 'By tapas, seek to know Brahman. Tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas. Having performed tapas —

ws.h: मन / mind / the thinking faculty
ws.e: mind / the thinking faculty — from √man (to think); manas = the faculty that processes sense-data, forms thoughts, desires, emotions; subtler than prāṇa because mind DIRECTS the vital force — prāṇa follows where mind leads; corresponds to the manomaya kośa

gr: Third realisation — mind (manas) is Brahman: Bhrigu's third tapas yields: MIND is Brahman. The reasoning: manas satisfies the triple criterion at the mental level: (1) Beings are 'born from' mind — in the sense that the desire to create (Brahman's 'bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'may I become many') is a mental act. Creation begins with THOUGHT. (2) Beings live by mind — conscious life is mental life; without mind, existence is not experienced. (3) Beings return to mind — at death, the individual mind merges back into the cosmic mind. Deeper than prāṇa: mind is more essential than breath because: (a) Mind DIRECTS breath — when you hold your breath or breathe deeply, it is the mind that commands. (b) Mind is the seat of experience — without mind, prāṇa is a blind force that sustains a body no one inhabits. (c) Mind includes AWARENESS — unlike prāṇa, which operates unconsciously, manas registers, processes, and responds to reality. Still incomplete: mind explains THOUGHT but not DETERMINATION. Manas is the wavering, doubting, processing faculty — it considers options but doesn't decide. The faculty that DETERMINES, JUDGES, and KNOWS with certainty is vijñāna (discernment) — a step beyond manas. Hence: more tapas.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.4.1 — Bhrigu's third realisation (manas = Brahman) corresponds to the manomaya kośa of the Brahmānandavallī (2.4). The claim that beings are 'born from mind' echoes the cosmogonic role of desire/thought in creation — the Nāsadīya Sūkta (Ṛg Veda 10.129.4) says 'kāmas tad agre samavartatādhi manaso retaḥ prathamaṁ yad āsīt' ('desire arose first in the beginning — the primal seed of mind'). Mind's limitation: in the Vedāntic analysis, manas is the PROCESSING faculty (saṁkalpa-vikalpa — considering and doubting), not the DETERMINING faculty (adhyavasāya — certainty). Brahman, being the ultimate reality, must be known with certainty, not merely considered. Hence vijñāna (determinate knowledge/discernment) is needed.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — मन = ब्रह्म — प्राण से सूक्ष्मतर (subtler than breath) — क्योंकि मन = चेतन (conscious) — सोचता, जानता, अनुभव करता है। परन्तु मन = संशयात्मक (doubting) — संकल्प-विकल्प (considering and doubting) — निश्चय (certainty) नहीं। ब्रह्म = निश्चित ज्ञान (certain knowledge) — मन से परे।
advaita.en: Shankara says mind = Brahman — subtler than breath — because mind = conscious — it thinks, knows, experiences. But mind = doubting — considering and reconsidering — not certainty. Brahman = certain knowledge — beyond mind.
advaita.ins: Bhrigu goes deeper still: mind is Brahman. Everything begins in thought, lives through experience, returns to consciousness. True — but mind wavers. It considers this, then that. It doubts. Brahman is beyond doubt. So: more tapas.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — मन = भगवान् का मानसिक रूप (God as mental consciousness) — प्राण से गहनतर। परन्तु मन = परिवर्तनशील (changing) — भगवान् = नित्य (eternal) — मन भगवान् का पूर्ण रूप नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says mind = God as mental consciousness — deeper than breath. But mind = changing — God = eternal — mind is not God's complete form.
vishisht.ins: God as mind — deeper than life-force, closer to the essence. Through mind, God thinks, experiences, knows. But the mind changes — one thought replaces another. God's nature is unchanging. Bhrigu must go deeper to find the stable core.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — मन = मानसिक चेतना (mental consciousness) — विचार, भावना, संकल्प (thought, emotion, will)। प्राणिक चेतना से ऊपर — परन्तु मन = विभाजनकारी (dividing) — यह एकता को खण्डों में तोड़ता है। सत्य-चेतना (truth-consciousness / vijñāna) = अखण्ड (undivided)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says mind = mental consciousness — thought, emotion, will. Above vital consciousness — but mind = dividing — it breaks unity into fragments. Truth-consciousness (vijñāna) = undivided.
aurobindo.ins: Mind is Brahman at the mental level — thought, experience, awareness. But mind divides — it separates subject from object, this from that, knower from known. The deeper plane — truth-consciousness — sees unity. Bhrigu must go past mind's divisions.

dp.q: 🔍 Mind as Brahman — the mental dimension
dp.a: Bhrigu's third realisation — manas (mind) = Brahman — represents the discovery of Brahman at the mental level: Why mind is deeper than breath: (a) Consciousness: mind introduces AWARENESS into the equation. Breath is a force; mind is an awareness. A breathing but unconscious body is alive but not experiencing life. Mind makes experience possible. (b) Direction: mind DIRECTS breath and body. You breathe faster when afraid, slower when calm — because mind shapes the vital force. The controller is more fundamental than the controlled. (c) Creation through thought: the Upanishads consistently describe creation as beginning with desire/thought — Brahman's 'may I become many' is a mental act. Mind precedes manifestation. Why mind is still incomplete: (a) Instability: manas wavers — it thinks one thing, then another. It doubts, reconsiders, oscillates. Brahman, as the ultimate reality, must be stable and certain. (b) Division: mind works by DIVIDING — subject vs. object, this vs. that, pleasant vs. painful. Brahman is ONE, undivided. Mind's very nature (analysis, discrimination) prevents it from grasping unity. (c) Processing vs. knowing: manas PROCESSES experience but doesn't DETERMINE truth. It considers options; vijñāna (discernment) decides. Brahman is not 'maybe this' — it IS. The progression so far: food (physical) → breath (vital) → mind (mental). Each layer is more subtle, more interior, more essential. But the journey is not yet complete — two more layers remain: knowledge (vijñāna) and bliss (ānanda).

dp.q: 🔍 The cosmogonic role of mind — desire before creation
dp.a: Bhrigu's insight that beings are 'born from mind' connects to a deep strand of Vedic cosmogony — the idea that creation begins with thought or desire: The Vedic evidence: (a) Nāsadīya Sūkta (Ṛg Veda 10.129.4): 'kāmas tad agre samavartatādhi manaso retaḥ prathamaṁ yad āsīt' — 'Desire arose first in the beginning — the primal seed of mind.' Before creation, there was desire — a mental event. (b) Taittirīya Brahmānandavallī (2.6.1): 'so'kāmayata bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'He desired: may I become many, may I be born forth.' Brahman's desire to create is a mental act — akāmayata (He desired) is a verb of mind. (c) Chāndogya (6.2.3): 'tad aikṣata bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'It saw/willed: may I become many.' Aikṣata (It saw/willed) is also mental. The implication: if creation begins with mind/desire/thought, then mind precedes the physical and vital worlds. Mind is more fundamental than food or breath because the universe itself is 'born from' a mental act. The limitation: even cosmic mind is not the ultimate — because mind operates through DISTINCTIONS (this vs. that), and the ultimate reality precedes all distinctions. The Nāsadīya Sūkta itself acknowledges this: 'ko addhā veda ka iha pra vocat' — 'who truly knows? who can declare it here?' Even mind reaches its limit when facing the Absolute.

sk: विज्ञानं ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात् विज्ञानाद्ध्येव खल्विमानि भूतानि जायन्ते विज्ञानेन जातानि जीवन्ति विज्ञानं प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्तीति तद्विज्ञाय पुनरेव वरुणं पितरमुपससार अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति तꣳ होवाच तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व तपो ब्रह्मेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा ||

hi: विज्ञानम् (knowledge / discernment / विज्ञान / विवेक-ज्ञान) = ब्रह्म इति व्यजानात् (he understood / उसने जाना)। विज्ञान से ही ये सभी भूत जायन्ते (are born)। विज्ञान से जातानि जीवन्ति (live)। विज्ञान में प्रयन्ति अभिसंविशन्ति (they enter back)। वह विज्ञाय पुनः वरुण पिता के पास गया। 'अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्म'। उससे कहा: 'तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व। तपो ब्रह्म।' उसने तपः किया। तप कर —
en: He understood: 'Knowledge/discernment (vijñāna) is Brahman.' For from vijñāna indeed these beings are born; by vijñāna, once born, they live; into vijñāna, departing, they enter. Having known that, he again approached his father Varuṇa. 'Teach me, revered sir, Brahman.' He said to him: 'By tapas, seek to know Brahman. Tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas. Having performed tapas —

ws.h: विज्ञान / विवेक-ज्ञान / discernment / direct knowledge / higher intellect
ws.e: discernment / direct knowledge / higher intellect — vi + √jñā (to know); vijñāna = discriminative knowledge — the faculty that DETERMINES, DECIDES, and KNOWS with certainty; deeper than manas (which considers and doubts), vijñāna settles and knows; it corresponds to buddhi (intellect) in its highest function and to the vijñānamaya kośa of the Brahmānandavallī

gr: Fourth realisation — knowledge (vijñāna) is Brahman: Bhrigu's fourth tapas yields: VIJÑĀNA (knowledge/discernment) is Brahman. The reasoning: vijñāna satisfies the triple criterion at the intellectual/cognitive level: (1) Beings are born from vijñāna — conscious creation requires intelligence; the cosmic intelligence (vijñāna) plans and executes creation. (2) Beings live by vijñāna — meaningful life is life guided by understanding, purpose, and discernment. (3) Beings return to vijñāna — at the deepest level, individual consciousness returns to cosmic intelligence. Deeper than manas: vijñāna transcends manas because: (a) While manas considers and doubts, vijñāna DETERMINES and KNOWS. It is the faculty of certainty vs. the faculty of consideration. (b) Vijñāna includes WILL — not just thinking but deciding and acting from knowledge. (c) The Brahmānandavallī describes vijñāna with spiritual qualities (śraddhā, ṛta, satya, yoga, mahas) — it is oriented toward TRUTH, not mere data-processing. Still incomplete: vijñāna explains KNOWING but not BEING. Knowledge is a faculty — it knows something. But the ultimate reality is not a faculty; it is a STATE OF BEING. What is the nature of being itself? The final answer — ānanda (bliss) — transcends even vijñāna because bliss is not something you KNOW but something you ARE.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.5.1 — Bhrigu's fourth realisation (vijñāna = Brahman) corresponds to the vijñānamaya kośa of the Brahmānandavallī (2.5). Vijñāna is philosophically significant because it represents the highest cognitive faculty — the ability to know with certainty, to discern truth from appearance. In the Brahmānandavallī, the vijñānamaya kośa is described with spiritual qualities (śraddhā, ṛta, satya, yoga, mahas) — suggesting that vijñāna at its highest IS spiritual discernment, not merely intellectual analysis. Yet even vijñāna is not the final answer: Shankara argues that vijñāna is still an instrument (karaṇa) — it is the MEANS of knowing, not the THING known. The thing known — the ultimate reality — is ānanda (bliss). Vijñāna is the last veil before the Self; ānanda is the Self's own nature.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — विज्ञान = ब्रह्म — मन से सूक्ष्मतर — निश्चयात्मक ज्ञान (determinate knowledge)। परन्तु विज्ञान = ज्ञान का साधन (instrument of knowledge) — ज्ञान का विषय (object of knowledge) नहीं। ब्रह्म = ज्ञान का विषय नहीं बल्कि ज्ञान का स्वरूप (the nature of knowledge itself) — आनन्द (bliss)।
advaita.en: Shankara says vijñāna = Brahman — subtler than mind — determinate knowledge. But vijñāna = an instrument of knowledge — not the object of knowledge. Brahman = not the object of knowledge but the nature of knowledge itself — bliss (ānanda).
advaita.ins: Bhrigu's fourth insight: knowledge itself is Brahman — certain, discriminating, truth-oriented. Deeper than wavering mind. But knowledge is still a TOOL — it knows something. What does it find when it turns fully inward? Bliss. One more round of tapas.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — विज्ञान = भगवान् का ज्ञान-रूप (God as knowledge/consciousness) — मन से गहनतर। भगवान् = सर्वज्ञ (omniscient)। परन्तु भगवान् = केवल ज्ञान नहीं — आनन्द भी (not just knowledge but also bliss)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says vijñāna = God as knowledge/consciousness — deeper than mind. God = omniscient. But God = not just knowledge but also bliss.
vishisht.ins: God as knowledge — omniscient, all-discerning. But God is not merely a knower — God is also bliss. Knowledge alone doesn't capture God's fullness. The final insight — bliss — completes the picture.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — विज्ञान = सत्य-चेतना (truth-consciousness) — मन से ऊपर का स्तर — सत्य का प्रत्यक्ष दर्शन (direct perception of truth)। परन्तु सत्य-चेतना = अभी भी ज्ञान (knowledge) — आनन्द-चेतना (bliss-consciousness) = और गहरा — चेतना का मूल स्वभाव।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says vijñāna = truth-consciousness — the plane above mind — direct perception of truth. But truth-consciousness = still knowledge — bliss-consciousness = even deeper — the fundamental nature of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Truth-consciousness — the plane where reality is seen directly, not through the dividing mind. But even direct knowledge is not the deepest layer. Beneath knowing is BEING — and the nature of being is bliss. One more descent inward.

dp.q: 🔍 Vijñāna vs. manas — knowledge vs. thinking
dp.a: The transition from manas (mind) to vijñāna (knowledge) represents a crucial shift from PROCESSING to KNOWING: Manas (mind): (a) Receives sense-data and forms initial impressions. (b) Considers options: 'is this a rope or a snake?' (c) Has doubts: saṁkalpa-vikalpa (considering and reconsidering). (d) Processes but does not determine. (e) Is reactive — it responds to inputs. Vijñāna (knowledge/discernment): (a) DETERMINES: 'this IS a rope' — settles the question. (b) DECIDES: makes choices based on understanding, not mere consideration. (c) Is certain: adhyavasāya (settled conviction). (d) Includes WILL — not just knowing but acting from knowledge. (e) Is proactive — it penetrates reality rather than merely receiving it. The Vedāntic distinction: in standard Vedāntic terminology, manas = the sense-mind (processing faculty) and vijñāna ≈ buddhi = the intellect (determining faculty). The Brahmānandavallī maps this distinction onto the kośa framework: the manomaya kośa processes (structured by the Vedas — external data), while the vijñānamaya kośa KNOWS (structured by faith, truth, yoga — internal qualities). Why vijñāna is closer to Brahman: vijñāna is the LAST cognitive faculty before bliss. It represents the highest capacity of the individual — the ability to know truth directly. In Sri Aurobindo's framework, vijñāna = supramental truth-consciousness — the plane where reality is seen whole, not divided by mind's analysis. It is the doorway to ānanda.

dp.q: 🔍 The penultimate station — why Bhrigu must go further
dp.a: Bhrigu's fourth realisation brings him to the very edge of the ultimate — vijñāna is the last veil before ānanda: What vijñāna gets right: (a) It is CONSCIOUS — unlike food and breath, vijñāna KNOWS. (b) It is CERTAIN — unlike mind, vijñāna doesn't waver. (c) It includes the faculty of WILL — vijñāna acts from knowledge, not from instinct or reaction. (d) It points toward truth — the Brahmānandavallī calls its wings ṛta and satya (cosmic truth and personal truth). What vijñāna still lacks: (a) It is still a faculty, not a state of being: vijñāna KNOWS reality; ānanda IS reality. The difference: a lamp illuminates a room, but light itself doesn't need illumination — it is self-luminous. Similarly, vijñāna illuminates truth, but ānanda (bliss) is the self-luminous nature of the Self. (b) It is relational: knowledge requires a knower and a known. Bliss transcends this duality — it is not the knowledge OF something blissful but the nature of BEING itself. (c) It answers 'how' but not 'why': vijñāna explains how we know, how we discern, how we determine. But WHY do we seek? WHY does anything exist? The answer — ānanda — is that existence exists because it IS bliss. The final step: Bhrigu will perform one more tapas and arrive at ānanda — bliss — the nature of Brahman itself. This is not another faculty but the ground of all faculties, the reason behind all seeking, the joy at the heart of being.

sk: आनन्दो ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात् आनन्दाद्ध्येव खल्विमानि भूतानि जायन्ते आनन्देन जातानि जीवन्ति आनन्दं प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्तीति सैषा भार्गवी वारुणी विद्या परमे व्योमन् प्रतिष्ठिता स य एवं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति अन्नवानन्नादो भवति महान् भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन महान् कीर्त्या ||
ro: ānandaḥ · brahma · iti · vyajānāt · ānandāt · hi · eva · khalu · imāni · bhūtāni · jāyante · ānandena · jātāni · jīvanti · ānandaṁ · prayanti · abhisaṁviśanti · iti · sā · eṣā · bhārgavī · vāruṇī · vidyā · parame · vyoman · pratiṣṭhitā · saḥ · yaḥ · evaṁ · veda · pratitiṣṭhati · anna-vān · anna-ādaḥ · bhavati · mahān · bhavati · prajayā · paśubhiḥ · brahma-varcasena · mahān · kīrtyā ||
hi: आनन्दः (bliss / आनन्द) = ब्रह्म (Brahman) इति व्यजानात् (he understood / उसने जाना)। आनन्द से ही (आनन्दात् हि एव खलु) ये (इमानि) सभी भूत (beings) जायन्ते (are born / जन्म लेते हैं)। आनन्द से (आनन्देन) जन्मे हुए (जातानि) जीवन्ति (live / जीवित रहते हैं)। आनन्द में (आनन्दम्) जाते हुए (प्रयन्ति) अभिसंविशन्ति (they enter back / प्रवेश करते हैं)। यह (सा एषा) भार्गवी (of Bhrigu / भृगु की) वारुणी (of Varuṇa / वरुण की) विद्या (knowledge / विद्या) है — परम व्योमन् (in the highest space / परम आकाश में) प्रतिष्ठिता (established / स्थापित)। जो (सः यः) इस प्रकार (एवम्) जानता है (वेद) — वह प्रतिष्ठित (established / दृढ़ प्रतिष्ठ) होता है। अन्नवान् (possessing food / अन्न-सम्पन्न) अन्नाद (eater of food / अन्न-भोक्ता) भवति (becomes / होता है)। महान् (great / महान्) होता है — प्रजया (in offspring / सन्तान से), पशुभिः (in cattle / पशुधन से), ब्रह्मवर्चसेन (in the radiance of Brahman-knowledge / ब्रह्मतेज से), महान् कीर्त्या (great in fame / कीर्ति से महान्)।
en: He understood: 'Bliss (ānanda) is Brahman.' For from bliss indeed these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss, departing, they enter. This is the knowledge of Bhrigu (bhārgavī), [taught by] Varuṇa (vāruṇī vidyā) — established (pratiṣṭhitā) in the highest space (parame vyoman). He who knows thus becomes established (pratitiṣṭhati). He becomes possessing food (annavān) and an eater of food (annāda). He becomes great (mahān) — in offspring (prajā), in cattle (paśu), in the radiance of sacred knowledge (brahma-varcas), great in fame (kīrti).

ws.h: आनन्द / परमानन्द / bliss / supreme joy
ws.e: bliss / supreme joy — ānanda is the final answer: Brahman IS bliss; the ultimate reality is not a thing, a force, a thought, or a concept, but BLISS — the nature of being itself is joy; this corresponds to the ānandamaya kośa and is the culmination of Bhrigu's five-fold inquiry

ws.h: भृगु-वरुण की विद्या / the knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuṇa
ws.e: the knowledge of Bhrigu (son of Bhṛgu) and Varuṇa — bhārgavī (of Bhrigu) + vāruṇī (of Varuṇa) + vidyā (knowledge/teaching); the name given to the entire teaching of the Bhṛguvallī; this vidyā is 'pratiṣṭhitā' (established) in the 'parame vyoman' (highest space) — connecting back to the Brahmānandavallī 2.1.1: 'nihitaṁ guhāyāṁ parame vyoman' (hidden in the cave, in the highest space)

ws.h: ब्रह्मतेज से / in the radiance of sacred knowledge
ws.e: in the radiance of sacred knowledge — brahma (Brahman/sacred knowledge) + varcas (radiance/lustre/splendour); the luminous power that comes from knowledge of Brahman; a person established in Brahman-knowledge shines with an inner radiance that is visible to others

ws.h: प्रतिष्ठित होता है / becomes established / becomes firmly grounded
ws.e: becomes established / becomes firmly grounded — prati + √sthā (to stand); the knower of this teaching becomes firmly established — unshakeable, rooted, stable; the same root as pratiṣṭhā (support/foundation) used throughout the kośa analysis

gr: Final realisation — bliss (ānanda) is Brahman: Bhrigu's fifth and final tapas yields the ultimate answer: ĀNANDA (bliss) is Brahman. The reasoning: ānanda satisfies the triple criterion at the deepest possible level: (1) Beings are born FROM bliss — the Brahmānandavallī (2.6) declared 'bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — Brahman's desire to become many arose from its own bliss/fullness. Creation is an overflow of joy. (2) Beings live BY bliss — the Brahmānandavallī (2.7) asked 'ko hyevānyāt kaḥ prāṇyāt' — 'who would breathe if bliss were not in space?' Bliss sustains all existence. (3) Beings return INTO bliss — at liberation (mokṣa), the individual self merges back into the infinite bliss of Brahman. Why ānanda is the final answer: (a) Ānanda is not a faculty (like vijñāna) but a STATE OF BEING — it is what Brahman IS, not what Brahman DOES. (b) Ānanda is self-validating — bliss does not need to be justified or explained; it is its own reason. (c) Ānanda answers the ultimate 'why?' — why does anything exist? Because existence IS joy. (d) Ānanda confirms the Brahmānandavallī's teaching: 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' — ananta (infinite) ≈ ānanda (bliss). The Bhārgavī-Vāruṇī Vidyā: this teaching is now given a formal name — the knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuṇa — established in the highest space (parame vyoman). The same 'parame vyoman' mentioned in the Brahmānandavallī's opening (2.1.1). The fruits: the knower of this teaching becomes established, possessing food, eating food, great in offspring, cattle, Brahman-radiance, and fame. These are not mere material rewards but signs of a life lived in harmony with the cosmic order.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.6.1 — Bhrigu's final realisation (ānanda = Brahman) is the culmination of both the Bhṛguvallī and the entire Taittirīya Upanishad. It confirms the Brahmānandavallī's teaching through independent discovery. The formal naming — 'bhārgavī vāruṇī vidyā' — elevates this from a father-son conversation to a named meditation tradition. The phrase 'parame vyoman pratiṣṭhitā' (established in the highest space) creates a direct link to the Brahmānandavallī 2.1.1: 'nihitaṁ guhāyāṁ parame vyoman' — the same 'highest space' that is both the cosmic empyrean and the cave of the heart. The fruits listed (annavān, annāda, mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ brahma-varcasena kīrtyā) represent the Vedic ideal of a complete life — material abundance AND spiritual radiance. This is characteristic of the Taittirīya: it does not oppose spiritual knowledge to material well-being but sees them as complementary. Notably, Varuṇa does NOT redirect Bhrigu this time — there is no 'do more tapas.' The silence IS the confirmation. Bhrigu has arrived.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — आनन्द = ब्रह्म — अन्तिम सत्य (final truth) — सत्-चित्-आनन्द (Sat-Chit-Ananda) का तीसरा पद। पाँच उत्तर: अन्न → प्राण → मन → विज्ञान → आनन्द = पाँच कोशों (five sheaths) के अनुक्रम में — स्थूल से सूक्ष्मतम तक। आनन्द = आत्मा का स्वरूप (the nature of the Self) — न कोश (not a sheath) — स्वयं ब्रह्म।
advaita.en: Shankara says ānanda = Brahman — the final truth — the third aspect of Sat-Chit-Ananda. The five answers: anna → prāṇa → manas → vijñāna → ānanda = in the order of the five sheaths — from grossest to subtlest. Ānanda = the nature of the Self — not a sheath — Brahman itself.
advaita.ins: Bhrigu's journey ends in bliss. Food, breath, mind, knowledge — each was Brahman at its level, each incomplete. But bliss IS Brahman — not another covering but the nature of being itself. Everything is born from joy, lives by joy, returns to joy. The search is over.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — आनन्द = भगवान् का स्वरूप (God's essential nature) = आनन्द-स्वरूप। पाँच स्तर = भगवान् के पाँच आयाम — अन्न, प्राण, मन, विज्ञान, आनन्द — सबमें भगवान् — सर्वान्तर में आनन्दमय भगवान्। 'भार्गवी वारुणी विद्या' = भगवद्-प्राप्ति का मार्ग (the path to God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says ānanda = God's essential nature = bliss-natured. Five levels = five dimensions of God — food, breath, mind, knowledge, bliss — God in all, God as bliss at the innermost. 'Bhārgavī Vāruṇī Vidyā' = the path to God.
vishisht.ins: God's deepest nature is bliss. Five layers of God's presence — food, breath, mind, knowledge, bliss — each deeper, each more luminous. At the core: God as pure bliss. Everything is born from His joy, lives by His joy, returns to His joy. Bhrigu has found the Beloved.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — आनन्द = चेतना का मूल स्वभाव (fundamental nature of consciousness) = सत्-चित्-आनन्द का तृतीय पद। पाँच स्तर = चेतना के पाँच स्तर — भौतिक → प्राणिक → मानसिक → सत्य-चेतना → आनन्द-चेतना। आनन्द = अस्तित्व का रस (the rasa of existence) — 'रसो वै सः' (Brahmānandavallī)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says ānanda = the fundamental nature of consciousness = the third aspect of Sat-Chit-Ananda. Five levels = five planes of consciousness — physical → vital → mental → truth-consciousness → bliss-consciousness. Ānanda = the rasa of existence — 'raso vai saḥ' (Brahmānandavallī).
aurobindo.ins: The deepest nature of consciousness is bliss — not an emotion but the fundamental taste of being. Five planes: matter, life, mind, truth, bliss. At the root: Ananda — the reason anything exists at all. Existence exists because it is joy. Bhrigu has touched the ground of all grounds.

dp.q: 🔍 Ānanda as Brahman — the culmination of the five-fold inquiry
dp.a: Bhrigu's final realisation — ānanda (bliss) = Brahman — is the climax of the Bhṛguvallī and the completion of the Taittirīya Upanishad's central teaching: The five realisations in sequence: (1) Anna (food) = Brahman at the physical level — TRUE but limited to matter. (2) Prāṇa (breath) = Brahman at the vital level — TRUE but limited to life-force. (3) Manas (mind) = Brahman at the mental level — TRUE but limited to thought. (4) Vijñāna (knowledge) = Brahman at the intellectual level — TRUE but limited to cognition. (5) Ānanda (bliss) = Brahman at the ultimate level — TRUE and COMPLETE. Why ānanda is the final answer: (a) It satisfies the triple criterion COMPLETELY: everything is born from bliss (creation is an overflow of joy), lives by bliss (bliss sustains all existence — 'ko hyevānyāt kaḥ prāṇyāt'), and returns to bliss (liberation = return to infinite joy). (b) It is not a FACULTY but a STATE OF BEING — unlike food, breath, mind, and knowledge, which are instruments or capacities, bliss is the NATURE of reality itself. (c) It is SELF-LUMINOUS — bliss doesn't need anything else to validate it. Joy is its own justification. (d) It connects the Bhṛguvallī to the Brahmānandavallī: the ānandamaya kośa was the innermost sheath, with Brahman as its pratiṣṭhā. Now Bhrigu has experientially confirmed what the Brahmānandavallī taught theoretically. The silence of Varuṇa: for the first time, Varuṇa does NOT say 'do more tapas.' His silence IS the confirmation. When the student reaches the truth, the teacher has nothing more to add.

dp.q: 🔍 The Bhārgavī Vāruṇī Vidyā — a named meditation tradition
dp.a: The Bhṛguvallī formally names its teaching the Bhārgavī Vāruṇī Vidyā (the knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuṇa), establishing it as a meditation tradition: What the name signifies: in the Upanishadic tradition, a 'vidyā' (knowledge/meditation) is not just information but a complete PRACTICE — a path of contemplation with a specific method and a specific goal. By naming this the 'Bhārgavī Vāruṇī Vidyā,' the Taittirīya transforms Bhrigu's personal discovery into a TRANSMISSIBLE tradition — anyone can follow the same path. The method of the vidyā: (1) Accept the triple criterion: Brahman = the source, sustainer, and goal of all beings. (2) Use tapas (concentrated contemplation) to investigate what satisfies this criterion. (3) Progressively deepen through five levels: food → breath → mind → knowledge → bliss. (4) At each level, test whether the answer is complete. If not, go deeper. (5) Arrive at ānanda — bliss — as the final, complete answer. 'Parame vyoman pratiṣṭhitā': this vidyā is 'established in the highest space' — the same 'parame vyoman' mentioned in the Brahmānandavallī's opening declaration ('nihitaṁ guhāyāṁ parame vyoman'). The highest space is both cosmic (the empyrean beyond all worlds) and personal (the innermost space of the heart). The vidyā is established there because its goal — ānanda — is both the cosmic absolute and the innermost self. The fruits: the knower becomes established, abundant in food, great in offspring, cattle, spiritual radiance, and fame. The Taittirīya does not set spiritual knowledge against material well-being — the two are complementary. The person established in ānanda naturally thrives in all dimensions of life.

sk: अन्नं न निन्द्यात् तद्व्रतम् प्राणो वा अन्नम् शरीरमन्नादम् प्राणे शरीरं प्रतिष्ठितम् शरीरे प्राणः प्रतिष्ठितः तदेतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितम् स य एतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति अन्नवानन्नादो भवति महान् भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन महान् कीर्त्या ||
ro: annaṁ · na · nindyāt · tat · vratam · prāṇaḥ · vā · annam · śarīram · anna-ādam · prāṇe · śarīraṁ · pratiṣṭhitam · śarīre · prāṇaḥ · pratiṣṭhitaḥ · tat · etat · annam · anne · pratiṣṭhitam · saḥ · yaḥ · etat · annam · anne · pratiṣṭhitaṁ · veda · pratitiṣṭhati · anna-vān · anna-ādaḥ · bhavati · mahān · bhavati · prajayā · paśubhiḥ · brahma-varcasena · mahān · kīrtyā ||
hi: अन्नम् (food) = न निन्द्यात् (one should not despise / निन्दा नहीं करनी चाहिए)। वह (तत्) व्रतम् (vow / व्रत / sacred resolution) है। प्राण (breath / प्राण) ही (वा) अन्नम् (food) है। शरीर (body) = अन्नाद (the eater of food / अन्न-भोक्ता)। प्राण में (प्राणे) शरीर (body) प्रतिष्ठित (established / स्थापित) है। शरीर में (शरीरे) प्राण प्रतिष्ठित है। इस प्रकार (तत् एतत्) यह अन्न = अन्न में (अन्ने) प्रतिष्ठित (established)। जो (सः यः) इस अन्न-में-अन्न-प्रतिष्ठित (food established in food) को जानता है (वेद) — वह प्रतितिष्ठति (becomes established / प्रतिष्ठित होता है)। अन्नवान् अन्नाद भवति। महान् होता है — प्रजया, पशुभिः, ब्रह्मवर्चसेन, महान् कीर्त्या।
en: One should not despise food (annaṁ na nindyāt). That is the vow (vratam). Breath (prāṇa) is food. The body (śarīra) is the eater of food (annāda). In breath, the body is established. In the body, breath is established. Thus food is established in food (annam anne pratiṣṭhitam). He who knows this — that food is established in food — becomes established. He becomes possessing food and an eater of food. He becomes great — in offspring, cattle, the radiance of sacred knowledge, great in fame.

ws.h: निन्दा नहीं करनी चाहिए / one should not despise / depreciate
ws.e: one should not despise / depreciate — na (not) + nindyāt (optative of √nind, to blame/despise); this begins a series of practical vows (vrata) regarding food; the first vow: NEVER despise food — because food is Brahman at the physical level, to despise food is to despise Brahman

ws.h: व्रत / sacred vow / resolution
ws.e: vow / sacred resolution — from √vṛ (to choose); a vrata is a solemn commitment to a specific practice; the Bhṛguvallī presents the anna-vrata (food-vow) as a practical application of Bhrigu's realisation — if food is Brahman, treat food with reverence

ws.h: अन्न अन्न में प्रतिष्ठित / food is established in food
ws.e: food is established in food — a paradoxical statement: prāṇa (breath) is food; the body is the eater of food; the body rests on breath, breath rests on the body — therefore food (in the form of breath) supports food (in the form of the body), and vice versa; the eater and the eaten are interdependent

gr: The first food-vow — do not despise food: after Bhrigu's five-fold realisation, the Bhṛguvallī shifts to PRACTICAL APPLICATION. The vow: 'annaṁ na nindyāt — tat vratam' — 'One should not despise food — that is the vow.' This is the first of several food-meditations that translate Bhrigu's insight (food = Brahman at the physical level) into daily practice. The logic of mutual support: prāṇa = food (prāṇa sustains life, just as food does). The body = the eater of food. But the body is established IN breath (without breath, the body is dead), and breath is established IN the body (without a body, breath has no home). Therefore: food supports food. The eater and the eaten are interdependent — a circle, not a hierarchy. The practical teaching: if food is Brahman, then: (a) NEVER despise food — what you eat is sacred. (b) Treat the preparation, sharing, and consumption of food as sacred acts. (c) Recognise the interdependence of all life through the food-cycle. The fruits: the standard formula — becoming established, possessing food, eating food, great in offspring, cattle, spiritual radiance, and fame.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.7.1 — The food-vows (mantras 7-10) are the Bhṛguvallī's practical section — they translate the theoretical realisation (ānanda = Brahman) back into daily life, starting with the most physical level (food). The first vow ('do not despise food') echoes the Brahmānandavallī's hymn to food (2.2): 'annaṁ hi bhūtānāṁ jyeṣṭham' (food is the eldest of beings). The paradox 'annam anne pratiṣṭhitam' (food established in food) is a meditation on MUTUAL DEPENDENCE: the eater (body) needs the eaten (food), and the eaten (food as breath/prāṇa) needs the eater (body as its vehicle). This circular interdependence reflects the Taittirīya's characteristic both-and logic — reality is not a linear hierarchy but a web of mutual support.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अन्नं न निन्द्यात्' = अन्न = ब्रह्म का स्थूल रूप — इसकी निन्दा = ब्रह्म की निन्दा। 'अन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितम्' = परस्पर-आश्रय (mutual dependence) — प्राण = अन्न (sustains like food), शरीर = अन्नाद (eater), दोनों परस्पर-आश्रित (interdependent)। व्यावहारिक शिक्षा (practical teaching) = ज्ञान को जीवन में उतारो।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'annaṁ na nindyāt' = food = the gross form of Brahman — despising it = despising Brahman. 'Annam anne pratiṣṭhitam' = mutual dependence — prāṇa = food (sustains), body = eater, both interdependent. Practical teaching = bring knowledge into daily life.
advaita.ins: After the highest realisation (bliss = Brahman), the Taittirīya returns to the humblest reality: food. Don't despise it. Food is Brahman's first face. Breath sustains the body; the body houses breath. Everything supports everything else. The sacred is not separate from the daily.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अन्नं न निन्द्यात्' = अन्न = भगवान् का रूप — भगवान् के किसी भी रूप की निन्दा = अपराध। भगवान् = अन्न में भी — प्राण में भी — शरीर में भी — सर्वत्र।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'annaṁ na nindyāt' = food = a form of God — despising any form of God = an offence. God = in food, in breath, in the body — everywhere.
vishisht.ins: Don't despise food — it is God's form. God is in what you eat, in the breath that sustains you, in the body that houses you. Everything is sacred because everything is God. This vow makes every meal a worship.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अन्नं न निन्द्यात्' = भौतिक जगत् (material world) की उपेक्षा नहीं — पदार्थ (matter) = चेतना का आधार (base of consciousness)। अध्यात्म (spirituality) = भौतिक जगत् का नकार नहीं बल्कि उसका रूपान्तरण (transformation, not rejection)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'annaṁ na nindyāt' = do not neglect the material world — matter = the base of consciousness. Spirituality = not rejection of the material but its transformation.
aurobindo.ins: The highest teaching returns to the humblest ground: don't despise food, don't despise matter. Consciousness needs a material base. The spiritual life doesn't reject the physical — it transforms it. Every meal, every breath, every bodily act can be a vehicle of the divine.

dp.q: 🔍 The food-vows — from realisation to practice
dp.a: After Bhrigu's climactic realisation (ānanda = Brahman), the Bhṛguvallī takes a surprising turn — it returns to food (anna) and offers a series of practical vows for daily life: Why return to food? Bhrigu's journey went from food (the lowest) to bliss (the highest). But the Taittirīya does not abandon the lower levels after reaching the highest. Instead, it RETURNS to the physical and TRANSFORMS it with the insight gained. This is the Taittirīya's characteristic both-and logic: (a) Ānanda is Brahman — the highest truth. (b) Anna is ALSO Brahman — the most immediate truth. (c) The sage who knows ānanda does not despise anna but REVERENCES it as Brahman's first face. The first vow: 'annaṁ na nindyāt — tat vratam' — do not despise food. This is not just dietary advice — it is a spiritual principle: if food is Brahman at the physical level, then despising food is despising a form of Brahman. Every meal becomes a sacred act. The mutual-support meditation: breath is food (it sustains like food). The body is the eater. But the body rests in breath, and breath rests in the body. Food supports food — a circle of interdependence. This meditation dissolves the hierarchy of eater and eaten, revealing them as two faces of one reality.

dp.q: 🔍 The circle of support — 'annam anne pratiṣṭhitam'
dp.a: The statement 'annam anne pratiṣṭhitam' (food is established in food) is a meditation on mutual dependence and the circularity of existence: The logic: (1) Prāṇa (breath) = anna (food) — because breath sustains life just as food does. (2) The body (śarīra) = annāda (the eater of food). (3) The body is established IN breath — without breath, the body is dead. (4) Breath is established IN the body — without a body, breath has no vehicle. (5) Therefore: food (as breath) supports food (as body), and food (as body) supports food (as breath). Food is established in food. The philosophical point: this is NOT a linear hierarchy (food at the bottom, bliss at the top) but a CIRCLE. The eater depends on the eaten, and the eaten depends on the eater. Subject and object are interdependent. This anticipates the Brahmānandavallī's insight: 'adyate atti ca bhūtāni' — food is eaten AND eats beings. The relationship is reciprocal. The practical implication: when you eat, you are not a sovereign consumer exploiting a passive resource. You and your food are in a relationship of MUTUAL SUPPORT. Someday your body will be food for the earth. This awareness transforms eating from consumption into communion — a participation in the great circle of existence.

sk: अन्नं न परिचक्षीत तद्व्रतम् आपो वा अन्नम् ज्योतिरन्नादम् अप्सु ज्योतिः प्रतिष्ठितम् ज्योतिष्यापः प्रतिष्ठिताः तदेतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितम् स य एतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति अन्नवानन्नादो भवति महान् भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन महान् कीर्त्या ||
ro: annaṁ · na · paricakṣīta · tat · vratam · āpaḥ · vā · annam · jyotiḥ · anna-ādam · apsu · jyotiḥ · pratiṣṭhitam · jyotiṣi · āpaḥ · pratiṣṭhitāḥ · tat · etat · annam · anne · pratiṣṭhitam · saḥ · yaḥ · etat · annam · anne · pratiṣṭhitaṁ · veda · pratitiṣṭhati · anna-vān · anna-ādaḥ · bhavati · mahān · bhavati · prajayā · paśubhiḥ · brahma-varcasena · mahān · kīrtyā ||
hi: अन्नम् (food) = न परिचक्षीत (one should not reject / refuse / त्याग नहीं करना चाहिए)। वह (तत्) व्रतम् (vow / व्रत) है। आपः (waters / जल) ही (वा) अन्नम् (food) हैं। ज्योतिः (fire/light) = अन्नाद (the eater of food)। जल में (अप्सु) ज्योतिः (fire/light) प्रतिष्ठित (established) है। ज्योतिष्यापः (in fire) आपः (waters) प्रतिष्ठित (established) हैं। इस प्रकार अन्न = अन्न में प्रतिष्ठित। जो इसे जानता है — वह प्रतिष्ठित होता है। अन्नवान् अन्नाद भवति। महान् होता है — प्रजया, पशुभिः, ब्रह्मवर्चसेन, महान् कीर्त्या।
en: One should not reject food (annaṁ na paricakṣīta). That is the vow. Waters (āpaḥ) are food. Fire/light (jyotiḥ) is the eater of food. In waters, fire is established. In fire, waters are established. Thus food is established in food. He who knows this — that food is established in food — becomes established. He becomes possessing food and an eater of food. He becomes great — in offspring, cattle, the radiance of sacred knowledge, great in fame.

ws.h: त्याग नहीं करना चाहिए / one should not reject / refuse / turn away
ws.e: one should not reject / refuse / turn away from — na (not) + pari + √cakṣ (to see/regard); literally 'not look away from' = don't refuse, don't reject food when it is offered or available; the second food-vow: while the first said 'don't despise,' this says 'don't refuse/waste'

ws.h: जल / waters
ws.e: waters — the cosmic element; here waters are identified as 'food' because water is essential nourishment — the basis of all life; the creation sequence (Brahmānandavallī 2.1) placed water between fire and earth

ws.h: अग्नि / प्रकाश / fire / light
ws.e: fire / light — the cosmic element; here fire is the 'eater' of water — fire evaporates water (consumes it), yet fire is also sustained by water (in the form of fuel/organic matter); mutual dependence again

gr: The second food-vow — do not reject food: the second vow shifts from inner attitude (don't despise) to outer action (don't refuse/waste). The vow: 'annaṁ na paricakṣīta — tat vratam' — 'One should not reject food — that is the vow.' While the first vow addressed mental attitude (contempt), this addresses physical behaviour (refusal/waste). The cosmic elements: this vow meditates on the ELEMENTS: water (āpaḥ) = food, fire (jyotiḥ) = the eater. Water and fire are interdependent: fire evaporates water (eats it), but fire depends on water-based fuel to burn (water sustains fire). Fire established in water; water established in fire. Food in food. The pattern: the same structure as the previous vow — a pair of cosmic elements, each supporting the other, demonstrating the mutual establishment of food in food.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_3.8.1 — The second food-vow uses a different pair of elements (water and fire) to demonstrate the same principle of mutual support. In the Vedic cosmology, fire and water are complementary opposites — fire transforms matter upward (through sacrifice/evaporation), water nourishes matter downward (through rain/irrigation). Their mutual dependence (fire evaporates water; water-based fuel sustains fire) mirrors the eater-eaten reciprocity. The vow 'na paricakṣīta' (don't reject) adds a practical dimension: don't waste food, don't refuse food offered to you, don't turn away from the nourishment that sustains life. Combined with the first vow ('don't despise'), it establishes a complete food-ethics: reverence (don't despise) + acceptance (don't reject).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'न परिचक्षीत' = अन्न का त्याग / बर्बादी नहीं — ब्रह्म के रूप में अन्न की स्वीकृति। आपः-ज्योतिः = जल-अग्नि = परस्पर-आश्रित — अग्नि जल को खाती है (वाष्पीकरण), जल अग्नि को पोषित करता है — अन्न अन्न में प्रतिष्ठित।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'na paricakṣīta' = don't reject/waste food — accept food as a form of Brahman. Water-fire = interdependent — fire consumes water (evaporation), water nourishes fire — food established in food.
advaita.ins: Don't refuse food — accept it as Brahman's gift. Water and fire depend on each other: fire drinks water, water feeds fire. The same circle again: food supports food. This vow turns every act of eating into recognition of the sacred interdependence of all things.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'न परिचक्षीत' = भगवान् के अन्न-रूप को अस्वीकार न करो — भगवान् का प्रसाद = अन्न। जल = भगवान् का पोषक रूप। अग्नि = भगवान् का रूपान्तरक रूप (transformative form)। दोनों = भगवान् के रूप।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'na paricakṣīta' = don't reject God's form as food — food = God's grace (prasāda). Water = God's nourishing form. Fire = God's transformative form. Both = forms of God.
vishisht.ins: Food is God's prasāda — don't refuse it. Water nourishes, fire transforms — both are God's forms. In their mutual support, God sustains God. Every drop of water, every flame of fire, every morsel of food is divine.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'न परिचक्षीत' = भौतिक जगत् को अस्वीकार नहीं — जल = जीवन-धारा (life-stream), अग्नि = रूपान्तरण-शक्ति (transformative power)। दोनों = चेतना के भौतिक रूप — परस्पर-आश्रित।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'na paricakṣīta' = don't reject the material world — water = the life-stream, fire = the transformative power. Both = physical forms of consciousness — interdependent.
aurobindo.ins: Don't refuse the material — it is consciousness in elemental form. Water flows and nourishes; fire transforms and consumes. They depend on each other. Every element is sacred, every physical process is consciousness at work.

dp.q: 🔍 Water and fire — the cosmic pair
dp.a: The second food-vow meditates on water (āpaḥ) and fire (jyotiḥ) as a pair of interdependent cosmic elements: Water as food: water is the most fundamental nourishment — more basic than solid food. All living beings require water. In the Vedic cosmology, water precedes earth in the creation sequence (Brahmānandavallī 2.1: agneḥ āpaḥ, adbhyaḥ pṛthivī). Water is the medium in which life first arose, and the substance without which no life can continue. Fire as the eater: fire 'eats' water — through evaporation, fire transforms liquid water into vapour. The digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) within the body 'eats' the water and food consumed, transforming them into energy. Fire is the principle of TRANSFORMATION — it converts one form into another. The mutual dependence: (a) Fire is 'established in' water — fire needs fuel, and all fuel is ultimately water-based (organic matter grows from water and earth). Without water, there is no fuel; without fuel, fire cannot exist. (b) Water is 'established in' fire — rain falls because the sun (fire) evaporates ocean water. Without solar fire, there would be no rain cycle, no fresh water. Water depends on fire for its circulation. The teaching: fire and water are not opposites but PARTNERS in the cycle of existence. Each sustains the other. This cosmic partnership mirrors the food-eater relationship: the eater needs the eaten, and the eaten (through the cycle of nature) needs the eater. All existence is mutual support.

dp.q: 🔍 The two food-vows compared — attitude and action
dp.a: The first two food-vows address two different dimensions of our relationship with food: First vow — 'na nindyāt' (don't despise): this addresses attitude. Don't hold food in contempt. Don't look down on the physical, the material, the bodily. This is an inner discipline — a shift in how we THINK about food. Second vow — 'na paricakṣīta' (don't reject): this addresses action. Don't refuse food when offered. Don't waste food. Don't turn away from nourishment. This is an outer discipline — a shift in how we ACT toward food. Together: the two vows create a complete food-ethics: (a) Inner: reverence for food as a form of Brahman. (b) Outer: acceptance of food, no waste, no refusal. The deeper principle: both vows flow from Bhrigu's realisation that food = Brahman at the physical level. If food is sacred, then despising it (inner) or wasting it (outer) is a form of irreverence toward the sacred. The Taittirīya's genius is to translate metaphysical insight into everyday behaviour — you don't just KNOW that food is Brahman; you LIVE that knowledge in how you eat, cook, share, and think about food.

sk: अन्नं बहु कुर्वीत तद्व्रतम् पृथिवी वा अन्नम् आकाशोऽन्नादः पृथिव्यामाकाशः प्रतिष्ठितः आकाशे पृथिवी प्रतिष्ठिता तदेतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितम् स य एतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति अन्नवानन्नादो भवति महान् भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन महान् कीर्त्या ||
